source.title: Towards Multimodal Interpretability: Learning Sparse Interpretable Features in Vision Transformers

record.tranche_reason: The post examines highest-activating images for MLP neurons, a neuron-level image-activation measure, on a CLIP vision transformer rather than the original InceptionV1 model.
record.gate_note: The neuron-level result is the statement that highest-activating images for all MLP neurons appeared to combine unrelated features. The SAE-feature alignment analysis, sparsity statistics, and feature-cluster results concern SAE features or their similarity to MLP vectors, not whether individual neurons respond to unrelated inputs, so they are not separate rows.
record.test_reason: The post inspects highest-activating images for MLP neurons in CLIP ViT Large. It reports that all of them appear to mix 3 or 4 unrelated features. That bears on V1 in a new setting: a vision transformer rather than the InceptionV1 convnet. The method is close to Zoom In's dataset examples, but the architecture differs, so T3 fits better than T1.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, but the emphasis differs. The main conclusion is that SAEs trained on a CLIP ViT residual stream find sparse, highly interpretable features. MLP-neuron polysemanticity is a brief side remark used to contrast neurons with SAE features. About half of the SAE features are not neuron-aligned under a crude cosine-threshold definition.
record.recipe_differences: Uses highest-activating images to assess MLP-neuron interpretability in CLIP ViT Large; the post does not present itself as a direct replication of the original InceptionV1 analysis.

fits_no_version.finding: SAE features in the layer-22 residual stream are far more interpretable than MLP neurons. About half are not aligned (cosine above 0.14) with any MLP-out vector, and the rest align with a few neurons, typically fewer than 5. None align with earlier-layer MLPs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Interpretable directions in vision transformers are often not neuron-aligned. This is consistent with superposition, but the post does not test it as a cause.

record.problems: The neuron interpretation is qualitative, without a stated scoring procedure or uncertainty. The post describes its neuron-alignment analysis as crude. The SAE was trained on ImageNet-1k and the reported neuron result does not state which layer or layers were inspected.
record.rows_left_out: No other reported result directly measures whether individual neurons respond to unrelated inputs.

untested.parts: InceptionV1 or other convnets, and specific canonical neurons such as the cat/car neuron. There is no quantified response strength, no feature visualisation of neurons, and no check that the mixed features are truly unrelated.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not one of the original sources. The neuron result is a single qualitative sentence with no counts, scoring method or examples shown, so the support for V1 is weak evidence. CLIP's vision encoder is not trained as a classifier; it is treated here as an image model within V1's scope.

versions.untested_parts: The post does not test InceptionV1 or neuron 4e:55 specifically; it reports on CLIP ViT Large. It does not quantify response strength.
Language-model neurons and token or context responses.
Whether capacity pressure or superposition causes neuron polysemanticity.
Polysemanticity arising from initialization, regularization, or training noise when capacity is sufficient.
Changes in polysemantic-neuron share across activation functions, architectures, or regularization, and any associated performance cost.
Whether apparently mixed neurons are explained by one shared feature or related offshoots of one job.
Whether polysemanticity depends on activation range or explanation-scoring choices.
